objectives: say exactly what changes when arithmetic becomes algebra: sentences stop asking "how much?" and start claiming "for every" — and letters are the machinery that makes the claim

classify any letter you meet into one of the four census roles — placeholder, generalizer, position letter, unknown — and name where each was first met (FM 11.2, FM 11.3, ANS 7.2) and where it grows next
state the three big laws in letter form and cash each on verified instances, knowing that the letter sentence covers every case while instances only sample it
evaluate expressions by substitution under the evaluation contract: replace every letter, honour the structure — and price the three classic traps (3a is 3 × a; a² is not 2a; −a flips the sign)
separate an expression (a name) from an equation (a sentence) by spotting the equals sign, and map the three jobs: simplify (rename), evaluate (fold), solve (settle)
recount who put letters into algebra — al-Khwārizmī's word algebra, Viète's 1591 system, Descartes' 1637 x, y, z — and why the change was worth a revolution

lessons.title: Expressions, Terms and Like Terms
concepts: The sign belongs to the term
Like terms and the letter part
objectives: take an expression apart by anatomy: name its terms, each term's factors and coefficient, and read the sign as part of the term — then name the family (monomial, binomial, trinomial)

draw the expression tree of a flat string and re-derive the order-of-operations conventions from it: brackets are the explicit override, multiplication assembles before addition, left-to-right settles the ties
decide like-or-unlike from the letter part alone, with the commutativity rescue for reordered products (3xy and 5yx are like; 3x and 3x² never are)

PROVE the collection law ax + bx = (a + b)x from the distributive law — first by the copies argument, then in full generality — and state honestly why unlike terms refuse to merge (the law needs a common factor)
simplify expressions by collecting like families and verify value-preservation by substitution: the name changes, the number never
price the merge-everything trap numerically: 3x + 5y is 21 at the witness (2, 3) while 8xy would claim 48 — collecting unlike terms is not shorthand, it is error

lessons.title: Evaluating Expressions: Substitution and Formulas
objectives: substitute at full strength into multi-term expressions, wrapping negatives in brackets so the tree of 1.2 folds exactly as drawn — (−3)² = 9, never −9
read a formula as a machine: one fold per input, a table for many inputs, and the honest habit of sanity-checking every output against its units
run four anchor-certified machines — the taxi C = 50 + 12k, the temperature pair C = (F − 32) × 5/9 and F = 9C/5 + 32, the triangle A = ½bh, the square perimeter 4s — and FM 11.2's dress Tn = 5n − 1
apply the standing speed method of 1.2: collect first, then fold, and know when a one-off substitution does not bother collecting
read a formula backwards by arithmetic undoing (which position holds 74?) as FM 11.2 did it — while keeping the general settlement for AL ch. 5
use evaluation as a lie detector: (a + b)² = a² + b² fails at EVERY pair in [1..10]², and one substitution kills a false identity on sight

lessons.title: Translating: Words into Symbols
concepts: The order traps: less than, divided by
objectives: use the translation dictionary lawfully: more than, times, of, per, less than, divided by — knowing which entries keep English order (subtraction and division) and which may flip (addition and multiplication)
price the order traps numerically: "5 less than x" is x − 5 (3 at x = 8), never 5 − x (−3); "the quotient of n and 3, increased by 1" is n/3 + 1 (5 at n = 12), never n/(3 + 1) (3)
resolve the two-readings trap with brackets: "twice the sum of x and 3" is 2(x + 3) = 14 at x = 4 while "the sum of twice x and 3" is 2x + 3 = 11 — same words reshuffled, different trees (1.2 cashed)
run the four-station translation pipeline — name the unknown, find the "is", translate phrase by phrase, plausibility-check — turning stories into lawful sentences
write the consecutive families (n, n + 1, n + 2; 2k, 2k + 2; 2k + 1, 2k + 3) and verify their sum laws by sweep
check every translation by substitution before trusting it: the candidate that satisfies the sentence survives, the one that fails is caught — the plausibility discipline of an examiner

chapters.title: Exponents and Powers
chapters.summary: Powers promoted from shorthand to system: the exponent laws (product, quotient, power-of-a-power) proved from the definition rather than drilled, then the family completed — zero and negative exponents as the same closure repair ANS performed on the number systems, with every old law preserved. Scientific notation and orders of magnitude pay the practical bill.

lessons.title: Powers and the Laws of Exponents
concepts: the sign law for negative bases
the exponent as a count of copies
the m > n boundary of the quotient law
objectives: read any power correctly — naming its base, its exponent and the copy count it compresses
prove the product, quotient and power-of-a-power laws from the definition by counting copies
verify each law on chosen numbers before trusting it, and say what the quotient law cannot yet do
handle zero, one and negative bases honestly — including the sign law and the bracket trap
apply the laws to simplify products, quotients and towers, and evaluate them at chosen values

lessons.title: Zero and Negative Exponents: Another Repair
concepts: the flip rule across the fraction bar
objectives: say precisely where the exponent family of 2.1 breaks, and why those breaks are diseases not flaws
derive x⁰ = 1 from the laws rather than accept it as a convention — and name the two routes that agree
derive x⁻ⁿ = 1/xⁿ from the repaired zero exponent, and move factors across a fraction bar both directions
verify that every law of 2.1 survives the extension, and evaluate expressions over all integer exponents
state the base-zero boundary honestly — which derivations die at zero, and why no repair can save them

lessons.title: Scientific Notation and Orders of Magnitude
concepts: the two dials of a number
objectives: convert any decimal — grotesquely large or vanishingly small — into the standard form a x 10^k with 1 <= a < 10
explain why the standard form is a NAME (unique per number) rather than a choice
multiply and divide in standard form using the exponent laws of 2.1 and 2.2, renormalising when the coefficient leaves [1, 10)
state what a coefficient claims about precision, and count its significant digits
compare numbers by exponent rungs — orders of magnitude — and say what that comparison hides

chapters.title: Polynomials
chapters.summary: The first algebraic family: what a polynomial is (terms, degree, classification by shape), arithmetic on polynomials — addition, subtraction and the distributive grid of multiplication — the special products (a ± b)² and (a + b)(a − b) PROVED by distribution and then used as identities, and division: long division as ANS’s division algorithm wearing letters, with the remainder theorem proved and the factor theorem glimpsed.

lessons.title: What a Polynomial Is: Terms, Degree and Family
objectives: define a polynomial term-by-term — a coefficient carrying a nonnegative integer power of the letter
read the anatomy of any term: coefficient, base letter, degree — and price why the coefficient never counts toward degree
classify polynomials by shape (monomial, binomial, trinomial, multinomial) and by degree (constant, linear, quadratic, cubic)
run the sieve: say exactly why 1/x, √x and 2^x are not polynomials, and why constants are
evaluate a polynomial at any value with the substitution machine, and build its value table
collect like terms at family scale and arrange answers in standard form

lessons.title: Adding, Subtracting and Multiplying Polynomials
objectives: add and subtract polynomials by degree-aligned column work, and prove the pointwise principle (f ± g)(x) = f(x) ± g(x)
multiply monomials, monomials by polynomials, and polynomials by polynomials on the distributive grid
collect the grid’s products on the convolution diagonal — the coefficient of xᵏ gathers every pair of degrees summing to k
prove deg(fg) = deg f + deg g by the leading-coefficient argument, and price the drop cases of deg(f ± g)
prove (a + b)² and (a + b)(a − b) by the grid, cashing the cross-term census of chapter 2
state the closure theorem — sums, differences and products stay in the family; quotients do not

lessons.title: Special Products: the Identities, Proved
concepts: trinomial squares and the middle-term test
objectives: state what an identity is — a sentence true for EVERY value of the letters — and distinguish identities from equations by testing values
read each square identity in both directions: expand the product form, and recognize the expanded form back into its product
derive (a − b)² twice — on the grid and by substituting −b into the square of a sum — and draw the corner-cut square that carries it
prove the sum and difference of cubes on the grid, cashing the (x − 1)(x² + x + 1) = x³ − 1 teaser of 3.2
apply the middle-term test to recognize trinomial squares and to refuse the impostors, and compute squares and products of numbers by identity instead of by column multiplication

lessons.title: Dividing Polynomials: Long Division and the Remainder Theorem
concepts: the division identity f = d·q + r
the stop rule: deg r < deg d
objectives: divide monomials by the index law — coefficients divide, exponents subtract — and divide polynomials by monomials term by term
run the long-division algorithm on polynomials arranged in descending (or ascending) powers, filling zero coefficients for missing degrees
state and prove the division identity f = d·q + r with deg r < deg d, and price why the quotient-remainder pair is unique
prove the remainder theorem from the division identity and use it to read remainders off values — evaluate, never divide
glimpse the factor theorem — f(a) = 0 forces (x − a) to divide f — as chapter 4’s opening engine

chapters.title: Factorization
chapters.summary: Multiplication undone, systematically: common factors and grouping as the two moves every factorization starts from, quadratic trinomials factored by the middle-term method with its existence justified, the special identities read backwards (difference of squares, perfect squares, sum and difference of cubes), and the factor theorem turning the remainder theorem into a cubic-hunting machine.

lessons.title: Common Factors and Grouping
concepts: the greatest common factor of terms
objectives: read the distributive law backwards — ca + cb = c(a + b) as the first factorization
compute the GCF of terms: the HCF of the coefficients wearing the shared letters at their lowest powers
extract the complete GCF, refuse partial extractions, and price the sign convention on negative leading coefficients
factor four-term expressions by grouping — pairing, the distributed minus, and the reorder when the natural pairing hides the match
state and use the honest boundary: a sum of squares refuses to factor over the integers, and say exactly why
check every factorization by expansion — the identity charter of 3.3 made into a habit

lessons.title: Factoring Quadratic Trinomials
concepts: the product dial and the sum dial
objectives: run the middle-term hunt on x² + px + q: find two integers whose product is q and whose sum is p
state and prove the gauge — the pair exists over the integers exactly when p² − 4q is a perfect square — and read its three verdicts
price the signs of the pair from the signs of p and q before hunting
factor ax² + bx + c (a ≠ 1) by the AC split, and close the split with 4.1’s grouping machine
extract the GCF first, recognize the 3.3 squares as the hunt’s double case, and refuse honestly when the gauge says no
verify every factorization by expansion — the ten-second identity check

lessons.title: The Identities as Factorizations
concepts: perfect squares via the zero gauge
objectives: read 3.3’s identity shelf backwards — each identity IS a factorization, and recognition is the art
recognize the difference of squares on sight, and refuse its sum-of-squares twin by the 4.1 theorem
recognize perfect squares by the middle-term test — the zero gauge of 4.2 wearing its other clothes
factor sums and differences of cubes, with the second bracket proved irreducible by the two-letter gauge
run the two-step chains (x⁴ − 16, x⁴ − 1, x⁶ − 1) until every factor is irreducible
apply the recognition order — GCF, squares and cubes, squares trinomials, the hunt, grouping — and meet the sum of fourth powers that factors after all

lessons.title: The Factor Theorem and Cubics
objectives: state and prove the factor theorem — (x − a) divides f(x) exactly when f(a) = 0 — from the remainder theorem, both directions
justify the candidate scan: every integer root of a monic cubic divides its constant term (proved), so the candidates are ± the divisors of d
run the cubic hunting machine: list candidates, evaluate (never divide), divide out the found root, and let the 4.2 toolkit finish the quotient
price the missing seat (x³ − 7x + 6 written 1, 0, −7, 6) and the repeated roots ((x − 1)²(x + 2))
prove and use the irreducibility verdict: a cubic with no integer root is irreducible over the integers — and meet what waits beyond (Cardano)
watch the two roads agree — the factor theorem re-deriving 3.3’s cube identities — and cash 3.1’s zero seed that planted this whole chapter

chapters.title: Linear Equations in One Variable
chapters.summary: The balance principle made lawful: an equation as an assertion, the moves that preserve truth justified by the field laws ANS proved, fractional and bracketed forms cleared systematically, and the three-way verdict — one solution, none, or infinitely many — read off the collapsed form 0·x = k, the same solvability discipline ANS 10.1 applied to the number ladder.

lessons.title: What an Equation Is: the Balance Principle
objectives: read an equation as an assertion to be settled — members, unknown, and the equals sign as the claim
sort assertions into identities, conditional equations and contradictions by a census of tested values, cashing 3.3’s identity charter
state the balance principle and the four lawful moves, each justified by the field laws ANS 7.2 proved
price the unlawful ×0 move that turns a false claim true — the trap the examinations set
use the solution-set language: solving means finding the WHOLE set, and the check by substitution confirms it
preview the three-way verdict — one, none, infinitely many — that 5.3 prices in full

lessons.title: Solving Linear Equations
objectives: run the five-station pipeline — clear fractions, clear brackets, collect, gather, divide — on any linear equation in one unknown
clear numeric fractions by multiplying every term by the LCD, and say WHY the move is lawful (the multiplier is never zero)
clear brackets with 3.2’s distributive craft, pricing the distributed-minus trap before it bites
collect like terms member-wise, gather the unknown onto one side, and divide by the coefficient — landing on the exact answer, fraction included
check every answer by substitution into the ORIGINAL equation, and watch the check catch real errors (the one-sided clearing among them)
connect the routine to its history — al-jabr’s restoring and al-muqābala’s confronting — and to its license, the move-equivalence law of 5.1

lessons.title: The Three Verdicts: One, None, Infinitely Many

chapters.title: Simultaneous Linear Equations

Word problems (age, mixture, cost) become the natural habitat of the method.

the slope-intercept form y = mx + b

books.title: Advanced Algebra
books.subtitle: Functions as objects — the second course
books.level: Class 11–12 algebra → the doorstep of calculus
books.description: The book where algebra grows up a second time. Foundation Mathematics opened the doorstep and Arithmetic and Number Systems proved the ground; Elementary Algebra opened the door and ended at the function idea. This book walks through: functions become objects — relations as sets of pairs, machines classified one-one and onto, composed in series with their honest domains, and undone by inverses. The quadratic returns as a working object — optimized, settled as inequalities on the sign diagram, mined for symmetric reads, its roots located in intervals. The extension ladder climbs its most famous rung: complex numbers built from a closure failure, carried by the field laws, and handed back to the quadratic formula so every discriminant is kept. Inequalities become the classical engine (AM–GM, Cauchy–Schwarz, the triangle inequality — proved, not recited). Sequences and series run from the constant climb to the infinite tail; counting becomes the exact science of permutations and combinations; mathematical induction certifies statements for every n at once; the binomial theorem is proved for a positive integral index and worked to its approximation power; the theory of equations counts roots, prices symmetric functions and transforms old roots into new equations; and the exponential and logarithmic family is defined once and for all as inverse machines. Cross-references Foundation Mathematics, Arithmetic and Number Systems and Elementary Algebra throughout; hands off to Coordinate Geometry, Trigonometry, Calculus and Probability.

chapters.title: Functions as Objects
chapters.summary: The book opens exactly where Elementary Algebra ended: the input-output machine becomes an object in its own right. First the set-of-pairs view — a relation as a subset of a product, a function as the special relation that is total and single-valued, the ground NCERT class 11–12 calls Relations and Functions and AL 11.3 never needed. Then the machine is classified: one-one, onto, the horizontal probe read at depth and the finite-set pigeonhole verdict. Then machines are wired in series — composition, its honest domain, its associativity, the identity — and finally undone: the inverse machine, when it exists, why existence is exactly one-one plus onto, and how the domain and range swap places. Piecewise-defined functions read honestly as machines with a switch; the transformation grammar — shifts, reflections, and the vertical and the horizontal stretch or squeeze — priced on the parent curves; and the craft of finding a function from a graph or a data table (the module’s problems based on finding function). This is the grammar every later chapter speaks.

lessons.title: Relations: the Set-of-Pairs View

relation as a chosen subset of A × B
the type census: empty, universal, identity, reflexive
the function as a total, single-valued relation

the honest domain of a composite
non-commutativity and the pairs that commute
counting composite pairs and distinct composites

existence = one-one AND onto (the bijective verdict)

the arithmetic and composition parity table

lessons.title: Unit Review: Functions as Objects
concepts: the arc of the chapter: the machine became an object — first a set of pairs, then a classified, wired, catalogued, tested, edited and measured object
the three standing verdicts: one-one (does it waste inputs), onto (does it cover the codomain), periodic (does it repeat)
bijective = one-one + onto = invertible — the promise the inverse lesson cashed
the counting census: 2^pq relations, n^m functions, the injection and surjection counts on small sets
the grammar of the chapter in one line: relation → function → verdicts → composition → inverse → zoo → parity → transformations → window
objectives: hold the whole chapter in one hand — the wiring of its eight lessons and where each promise was cashed

chapters.title: The Quadratic at Depth
chapters.summary: Elementary Algebra settled the quadratic equation four ways; this chapter treats the quadratic as a working object. The vertex form becomes an optimization tool — maxima and minima priced without calculus, the range read off the fold and then used on real constraints. The equation grows into the inequality: the sign diagram, the discriminant trichotomy (two sign changes, one touch, constant sign), and the solution sets that AL 7.1–7.3’s linear work promised. Viète returns at competitive depth — symmetric expressions in the roots, common roots, forming equations with given roots — and the chapter closes with the JEE classic: conditions that pin both roots, or exactly one, inside a chosen interval. Every door metaphor AL coined for a root is now located on the line.

chapters.title: Complex Numbers: the New Rung
chapters.summary: Arithmetic and Number Systems proved the extension-ladder discipline — every new number family born from a closure failure, repaired on purpose. This chapter climbs the most famous rung: x² + 1 = 0 has no real door, so a number i is forced with i² = −1, and the algebra of a + bi is built so the whole field-law family survives (the honest sanity ANS 7.2 banked). The conjugate and modulus arrive as bookkeeping — z z̄ = |z|², division by conjugating, |z| as a distance with the triangle inequality — and the Argand plane is read algebraically (addition as the parallelogram, multiplication as rotation-and-scaling) with the deep geometry left to later books. The payoff: the quadratic formula keeps its promise for every discriminant, and real coefficients are shown to force complex doors in conjugate pairs. De Moivre’s theorem and the nth roots of unity — the unit circle’s equal spokes — with their properties (primitive roots, the cyclotomic equations) banked as the module’s depth engine.
plannedLessons: The Closure Failure That Forces i
Negative Discriminants: the Doors Turn Complex
The Argand Plane: Polar Form and the Argument
De Moivre, Roots of Unity and the Complex Loci

chapters.title: Inequalities: the Classical Engine
chapters.summary: AL chapter 7 settled order on the line for linear expressions; this chapter builds the classical machinery that competitive exams actually test — maxima and minima without calculus. The arithmetic–geometric mean inequality is proved for two numbers from the square that is never negative, stated honestly beyond, and worked under constraints (the fixed-sum, fixed-product discipline). Cauchy–Schwarz arrives with its Engel (Titu) form, the speed tool for fraction sums. And the absolute value FM priced as distance becomes a bound machine: |f| < g and |f| > g verdicts, the triangle inequality proved, and the |x| + |y| ≥ |x + y| reads that finish the engine. Every result is derived before it is used — the AM–GM equality condition is a theorem about when two numbers coincide, not a memorized footnote.
plannedLessons: The Weighted AM-GM and Its Consequences
Absolute Value at Depth: the Triangle Inequality

chapters.title: Sequences and Series
chapters.summary: Lists with structure become algebra: the arithmetic progression as a constant climb (its nth term, its sum, the means inserted between numbers), the geometric progression as a constant ratio (its sum, and the infinite tail |r| < 1 — the book’s first honest limit, the doorstep Calculus will formalize), then the cousins: the harmonic progression read as reciprocals of a climb, and the arithmetico-geometric progression the JEE syllabus names explicitly. The chapter closes with the special sums Σk, Σk², Σk³ — proved the honest way first (the pairing trick FM 11.2 would recognize), with the method of differences and telescoping as the general craft for series whose terms surrender their middles. The induction certificate for these sums is deliberately deferred to chapter 7, exactly where the classics put it. Sigma notation for dependent and for independent index variables — the compression every later series argument writes with — named and priced here.
plannedLessons: Geometric Progressions and the Infinite Tail
Special Series and the Method of Differences
Sigma Notation and the Classical Power Sums
Recurring Series and the Scale of Relation

chapters.title: Counting: Permutations and Combinations
chapters.summary: Algebra’s discrete half: counting as an exact science, the way both the JEE module and Hall & Knight teach it — the fundamental principle first (multiply along a chain of independent choices, add across mutually exclusive alternatives), then the two great counts derived rather than memorized: the permutation as an arrangement (nPr from the chain itself, factorials, arrangements of alike things, the circle), and the combination as a selection (nCr, its symmetry and complement reads, choosing from groups). The chapter closes with the distribution puzzles — words into boxes, people into rooms, at-least and at-most selections — where the two principles interlock and a wrong model is caught by the small-case census. Circular permutations — the round table and the necklace — with the clockwise and anticlockwise arrangements priced exactly; the distribution of identical objects and of distinct objects into groups, with and without empty groups allowed; and the properties of nCr (symmetry, absorption, Pascal’s identity) derived, not quoted. This is the ground Probability inherits, and it is built to be inherited honestly.
plannedLessons: Distributions and the Classic Counting Puzzles

chapters.title: Induction and the Binomial Theorem
chapters.summary: The book’s proof engine and its most-used consequence, in the order the classics teach them. Mathematical induction first — the domino principle: base case, inductive step, and the honest scope note (what induction proves and what it never can), applied to the sum formulas chapter 5 left uncertified, to divisibility statements, and to inequality statements the AM–GM engine guessed. Then the binomial theorem for a positive integral index — Pascal’s triangle read as a counting statement about chapter 6’s selections, the theorem PROVED by induction, the general and middle terms priced exactly. The coefficients become objects of study (their sum, their alternating sum, the term independent of x), and the chapter closes with the applications: (1 + x)ⁿ ≈ 1 + nx for small x, divisibility reads, and coefficient-hunting at exam speed. The frequently used expansions — (a ± b)², (a ± b)³ and the kin every exam expects by reflex — banked as the chapter’s opening toolkit.
plannedLessons: The Binomial Theorem for Any Index

chapters.title: The Theory of Equations
chapters.summary: The polynomial’s deepest algebra — Hall & Knight’s heartland, entered honestly. How many roots a degree-n equation truly has: n over the complex numbers (the fundamental theorem stated, not proved — with the honesty the platform owes its readers), multiplicities counted, and the conjugate-pair law for real coefficients derived from chapter 3’s algebra rather than asserted. Viète generalizes: the symmetric functions of a cubic’s and a quartic’s roots, the sum–sum-of-products–product staircase, and what symmetric reads survive when the roots are not nice. The chapter closes with the transformation craft: build the equation whose roots are the old roots shifted, scaled or inverted — the classic technique that turns hard cubics into transparent ones and reciprocal equations into quadratics in disguise.
plannedLessons: How Many Roots: Degree n, n Roots
Cubics and Quartics: the Symmetric Functions
Cardan and Ferrari: the Cubic and Quartic, Solved

chapters.title: Exponentials and Logarithms
chapters.summary: The first great non-polynomial family inside algebra. The exponent laws AL banked on integer and rational indices are extended to every real index — the exponential function aˣ as a machine with a constant percent climb, its shape family, and the growth stories it prices. The logarithm is then defined once and for all as the inverse machine — chapter 1’s theory cashing its first big cheque: domain and range swap, log_a(aˣ) = x, and every log law DERIVED from the exponent law it mirrors instead of memorized. Change of base, the common and natural logarithms, and the chapter closes on equations: same-base discipline, exponent equations that hide quadratics, log equations with their domain discipline enforced (extraneous roots caught, not mourned), and the growth and decay problems that make the family famous.
plannedLessons: The Exponential Family: Every Real Index
The Laws of Logarithms and the Change of Base
Logarithm Tables: Characteristic, Mantissa and Antilogarithm

chapters.title: The Synthesis and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The closing synthesis, in the house manner. First the competition craft across all the new families — the substitution game on quadratics and symmetric reads, AM–GM maxima under constraints, series sums priced by difference and telescoping, binomial term hunts, log speed reads — the advanced sequel to AL 11.2. Then the book in one page: the honest map of what was built and what was only opened, the cross-references made good, the formula family gathered. And then the doorstep itself: the infinite tail’s limit met again, the changing output measured discretely along the new families (slopes of aˣ and log taken the honest, finite way AL 10.2 priced for lines), continuity named as a promise — the handoff to Calculus, with Coordinate Geometry (graphs reunited) and Trigonometry (the next family) named as the neighbouring doors.
plannedLessons: Functional Equations: Building Functions from Rules
The Book in One Page: Synthesis
The Doorstep: Limits and the Changing Output

books.title: Geometry
books.subtitle: Shapes with reasons — the proof-driven classical course
books.level: Class 6–10 geometry → the olympiad doorstep
books.description: The book where mathematics becomes proof. Foundation Mathematics banked the shapes and their measures; this book rebuilds geometry the way Euclid did — undefined words, postulates, and theorems earned one argument at a time. Congruence and the triangle criteria, similarity and a Pythagoras that is finally proved, the parallelogram family, the circle theorems olympiad problems run on, the ruler-and-compass discipline the rationalized syllabus dropped, Heron’s formula and the solids — every formula either proved or honestly flagged. The book closes on the ideas that broke and rebuilt the subject: equivalents of the parallel postulate, Hilbert’s rigour repair, and the non-Euclidean geometries born from denying Euclid’s fifth. Cross-references Foundation Mathematics throughout; hands off to Coordinate Geometry, Trigonometry and the olympiad ladder.

chapters.title: Points, Lines and Planes: the Axiomatic Idea
chapters.summary: Geometry restarts from zero — not from shapes but from RULES. The undefined words (point, line, plane), the definitions that ride on them, and Euclid’s five postulates as the rules of the game. The reader meets the axiomatic method itself: a statement is believed only when proved, and everything before the first proof is either an agreement or a promise. Foundation Mathematics 8’s shape vocabulary is recalled as the intuition this structure formalises.
plannedLessons: The Undefined Words and the Defined Ones
Euclid’s Five Postulates: the Rules of the Game
Axioms, Theorems and the Shape of a Proof
Incidence: how Points, Lines and Planes Interlock

chapters.title: Angles, Parallel Lines and the Transversal
chapters.summary: Angles measured, named and paired; then the parallel line and the transversal — the eight-angle census (corresponding, alternate, co-interior) that powers half of school geometry. The angle-sum of a triangle is DERIVED from the parallel postulate, and the exterior-angle inequality follows — the first classic theorems proved the honest way.
plannedLessons: Parallel Lines and the Fifth Postulate
Angle Sum of a Triangle and Its Consequences

chapters.title: Triangles: Congruence and the Craft of Proof
chapters.summary: The chapter that makes geometers: congruence as exact coincidence, the five criteria (SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS, RHS) stated as postulates-of-method and used with discipline, and the classic consequences PROVED — isosceles triangles, the equilateral case, and the side/angle inequalities. Every proof is written the Euclidean way: statement, construction, argument, conclusion.
plannedLessons: Congruence: the Idea of Same Shape and Size
The Congruence Criteria: SAS, ASA, AAS, SSS, RHS
Inequalities in a Triangle: Sides and Angles
The Cevian Theorems: Ceva and Menelaus
Stewart’s Theorem and the Median Relation

chapters.title: Similarity: the Geometry of Proportion
chapters.summary: Foundation Mathematics 6’s ratio and proportion return as geometry’s scaling law. The Basic Proportionality (Thales) theorem proved, the similarity criteria (AA, SAS, SSS) built on it, and Pythagoras’s theorem PROVED by similarity and again by areas — the theorem the reader has used since Foundation Mathematics is finally earned. Areas scale as the square of the ratio; volumes as the cube.
plannedLessons: Similar Figures: Same Shape at Any Scale
The Similarity Criteria: AA, SAS, SSS

chapters.title: Transformations and Symmetry: the Rigid-Motion Idea
chapters.summary: Congruence and similarity earn their machine definitions: translations, reflections and rotations written as functions of the plane — the rigid motions — their compositions read as the isometry idea, line and rotational symmetry found as the fixed sets of those motions, and dilations as the scale engines that re-derive similarity. The Common Core’s transformation-first route and NCERT’s symmetry chapters are both honoured: SAS/ASA/SSS are re-read as invariances under motion, and the ground is laid for the homothety reading of centres of similitude in the circle chapter and for the shifting of axes in Coordinate Geometry.
plannedLessons: The Rigid Motions: Slides, Flips and Turns
Composing Transformations and the Isometry Idea
Dilations, Scale Factors and Similarity Re-Read

chapters.title: Quadrilaterals and Polygons
chapters.summary: The parallelogram family — parallelogram, rectangle, rhombus, square, trapezium — with its diagnoses proved from triangle congruence. The midpoint theorem (and its converse) as the classic consequence, and polygons in general: interior/exterior angle sums, regular polygons, diagonals. The trapezium midsegment closes the chapter as similarity’s first application.
plannedLessons: The Midpoint Theorem and the Trapezium

chapters.title: The Circle: Chords, Angles and Tangents
chapters.summary: The circle read the classical way: chords and arcs, the angle-at-the-centre theorem, angles in the same segment, the cyclic quadrilateral and its opposite angles, tangents and the alternate-segment theorem. Every result proved from congruence and the angle census — the theorems that olympiad geometry actually runs on.
plannedLessons: Chords and Arcs: the First Circle Theorems
Angles in a Circle: Centre, Circumference, Segment
Tangents and the Alternate Segment Theorem
Common Tangents and Centres of Similitude
The Nine-Point Circle and Euler’s Line

chapters.title: Ruler-and-Compass Constructions
chapters.summary: The discipline the rationalized textbook dropped and the classic canon keeps: constructions with unmarked straightedge and collapsing compass — bisectors, perpendiculars, triangles from given parts, tangents to circles, similar figures. Each construction ends with its PROOF that the figure has the required property; the impossible constructions (trisecting a general angle) are named honestly and deferred to the algebra that explains them.
plannedLessons: Tangents and Similar Figures by Construction
Inscribed, Circumscribed and the Regular Polygons

chapters.title: Areas: Heron’s Formula and the Plane Region
chapters.summary: Area as a proved quantity: rectangles and parallelograms from the axioms, triangles, and Heron’s formula derived (the algebra of AL and the surd craft it banked doing the work). Then the circle’s regions — sector, segment — with the area and circumference limits met honestly (the first limit in the shelf since Advanced Algebra’s infinite tail, and a doorstep Calculus will formalise). Combinations of plane figures complete the aptitude-exam scope.
plannedLessons: Areas of Rectangles, Parallelograms and Triangles
Sectors, Segments and Combinations of Figures

chapters.title: Surface Areas and Volumes
chapters.summary: The third dimension: prisms and cylinders, pyramids and cones, spheres and hemispheres — each formula either proved by dissection (Cavalieri’s principle stated honestly) or flagged as a fact whose proof belongs to calculus. Frustums and combinations of solids complete the aptitude and board scope; the cone/sphere limit arguments open the door Integral Calculus will walk through.
plannedLessons: Spheres, Hemispheres and Combinations of Solids

chapters.title: Proof, the Postulates and the Non-Euclidean Door
chapters.summary: The chapter the shelf owes its most curious readers: equivalents of the parallel postulate (Playfair’s form, the angle-sum statement), Hilbert’s repair of Euclid’s gaps, the discovery that the fifth postulate cannot be proved — and that denying it builds honest geometries (spherical/elliptic and hyperbolic, with Gauss, Lobachevsky and Bólyai named). History verified, not folklore; the door to differential geometry named.
plannedLessons: Equivalent Forms of the Parallel Postulate
The Non-Euclidean Door: when Parallel Lines Misbehave

chapters.title: The Synthesis and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The closing synthesis in the house manner: competition geometry craft (the auxiliary line, the construction you add, the diagram census — olympiad-style worked problems at graded levels), the book in one page (the theorem map from postulates to volumes), and the doorstep itself: figures acquire addresses — Descartes’s idea — handing off to Coordinate Geometry, with Trigonometry named as the triangle’s measuring instrument.
plannedLessons: The Book in One Page: the Theorem Map

books.title: Coordinate Geometry
books.subtitle: Figures with addresses — algebra owns the plane and space
books.level: Class 9–12 analytic geometry → the calculus doorstep
books.description: The book where geometry and algebra fuse completely. The coordinate system and the locus idea; straight lines in every form; the pair of lines; the circle with its radical-axis theory; the three conics — parabola, ellipse, hyperbola — each with tangents, normals, parametric forms and famous properties; then the unified conic family with eccentricity as the dial. The third dimension follows: points, spheres and direction cosines, vector algebra with its three products, and lines and planes in space including skew lines. Every formula derived; Geometry’s theorems cross-referenced where the algebra leans on them; Advanced Algebra’s quadratic work cashed as the second-degree family. Cross-references Elementary Algebra, Geometry, Advanced Algebra and Trigonometry; hands off to Differential Calculus, with Multivariable Calculus named as the sequel.

chapters.title: The Coordinate System and the Locus Idea
chapters.summary: Elementary Algebra’s graphs become a precise instrument: the rectangular axes, transformation of axes, the distance formula and the area of a polygon, the section formula (internal and external), the centres of a triangle (centroid, circumcentre, orthocentre, incentre, excentres), slope, polar coordinates, and the locus — the curve as the set of points that satisfy a condition, its equation found by elimination. Every formula proved, not quoted; Geometry’s figures now carry addresses. The section formula priced once for internal division and once for external — the one machine behind every centre-of-gravity and ratio-point problem.
plannedLessons: Axes, Quadrants and the Address of a Point
Distance, Section and the Area of a Polygon
The Centres of a Triangle in Coordinates

chapters.title: Straight Lines
chapters.summary: The line algebraically owned: slope and its readings, every standard form of the equation (slope-intercept, point-slope, two-point, intercept, normal), the angle between two lines, concurrency conditions, the distance of a point from a line, the family of lines through an intersection, and the shifting of axes. The JEE workhorse chapter — built with every formula derived from the two foundations: slope and the distance formula.
plannedLessons: Slope and the Forms of a Line’s Equation
Shifting the Axes: Transformation to Origin
Rotation of Axes and the Invariants

chapters.title: Pair of Straight Lines
chapters.summary: Two lines in one equation: the general second-degree equation that factors, the homogeneous second-degree equation through the origin, the angle between the pair, the combined equation of the angle bisectors, and homogenization — the craft of pairing a curve with a pair of lines through the origin. A short, sharp chapter that arms the conic chapters ahead.

chapters.title: The Circle
chapters.summary: Geometry’s most symmetric figure, now computed: centre-radius and general forms, circles touching the axes, three-point circles, the parametric form, position of a point, line–circle intersections, the tangent and normal in all their forms, the pair of tangents, chord of contact, director circle, and the two-circle theory — radical axis, radical centre, and every contact case priced. Geometry’s chapter-6 theorems cross-referenced wherever the algebra leans on them. The secant of a circle — the chord’s limiting shadow — named so tangent theory never floats free of its parent.
plannedLessons: The Equation of a Circle in All Its Forms
Position, Intersection and the Length of a Tangent
Two Circles: the Radical Axis and Contact Cases
Orthogonal and Coaxal Systems of Circles

chapters.title: The Parabola
chapters.summary: The first conic, met as the locus of a point equidistant from focus and directrix: the standard equation and its four forms, shifted axes, focus–directrix constructions, the focal chord and its properties, position of a point, the parametric form, tangents (all forms), the pair of tangents, properties of tangents, normals from an external point, and conormal points. Advanced Algebra’s vertex-form optimization cross-referenced — the parabola is the same object both books claim.
plannedLessons: Focus, Directrix and the Standard Parabola
Focal Chords and the Parametric Form
Tangents and Normals to the Parabola

chapters.title: The Ellipse
chapters.summary: The stretched circle: standard equations in every orientation, axes-parallel forms, eccentricity, the focal property, auxiliary and director circles, the parametric form, position of a point, chords bisected at a point, tangents and normals (all forms), and the reflection property that makes the ellipse famous in physics. Areas by the elliptical formula meet Integral Calculus’s doorstep honestly.
plannedLessons: The Standard Ellipse and Its Anatomy
Tangents, Normals and the Reflection Property
Diameters, Conjugate Diameters and the Auxiliary Circle

chapters.title: The Hyperbola
chapters.summary: The conic with two branches: standard and shifted equations, eccentricity, focal chords, the auxiliary circle, the parametric form, tangents and normals, the asymptotes — tangents at infinity — with their properties, and the rectangular hyperbola referred to its asymptotes as axes. The chapter the calculus doorstep borrows for curve sketching.
plannedLessons: The Standard Hyperbola and Its Branches

chapters.title: The Conic Family Unified
chapters.summary: The synthesis chapter the module’s arc earns: one focus–directrix definition with eccentricity as the dial (0 circle → <1 ellipse → 1 parabola → >1 hyperbola), the general second-degree equation identified (the discriminant census, cross-referenced with chapter 3’s pair-of-lines case), tangents/normals/chord of contact written once for all conics, and the polar equation preview named. The family portrait before dimension three.
plannedLessons: Tangents and Chords of Contact, Unified
The Director Circle: One Idea across the Conics
The Normals from a Point: Three and Four
Confocal Conics and Families of Conics

chapters.title: The Third Dimension: Points, Spheres and Directions
chapters.summary: Space acquires coordinates: the three mutually perpendicular planes, coordinates of a point, direction angles and direction cosines, planes perpendicular to axes and lines parallel to them, the distance formula, the section formula, and the sphere’s equation. The M5 module’s opening ground — built carefully, because everything in chapters 10–12 stands on it.

chapters.title: Vector Algebra: Arrows with Rules
chapters.summary: The vector as a quantity with magnitude and direction: position vectors, types, addition (the parallelogram law), components, scalar multiplication, the vector joining two points, the section formula in vectors, the bisector vector, linear combinations, and the honest ground of linear dependence and independence — the idea Linear Algebra will generalize. Drawn as arrows, computed as triples. Linearly dependent and independent vector sets priced on triples with the collinearity/planarity verdicts that follow.
plannedLessons: Addition, Scalar Multiplication and the Section Formula

chapters.title: The Products of Vectors
chapters.summary: The three products that make vectors an instrument: the dot product (physical and geometric meaning, properties, angle work and projections), the cross product (area meaning, the moment of force, properties), the scalar triple product (coplanarity and the volume of a tetrahedron) and the vector triple product with Lagrange’s identity. The module’s deepest chapter — and the shelf’s cleanest bridge into physics. The geometrical interpretation of the scalar product — the projected-length reading — derived first, so work, angles and projections share one spine.
plannedLessons: The Dot Product: Angles and Projections
The Cross Product: Areas and Moments

chapters.title: Lines and Planes in Space
chapters.summary: The JEE unit-5 heartland: equations of a line (through a point along a vector; through two points), the angle between two lines, points on lines, the shortest distance between lines — skew lines included — and every form of the plane’s equation (normal, three-point, through a point parallel to two vectors, intercept), line–plane and plane–plane angles, distances of points from planes, and the family of planes. Chapter 9’s direction cosines and chapter 11’s products doing all the work. The regular tetrahedron — its height, its symmetric product identities — the shelf’s flagship 3D solid, priced exactly.
plannedLessons: The Plane in All Its Forms
Angles and Distances: Lines, Planes, Skew Lines

chapters.title: The Synthesis and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The closing synthesis: competition craft (locus problems, parametric conics, the 3D short-distance hunt — worked at graded levels with the module’s exam typology), the book in one page (the coordinate map from locus to plane), and the doorstep itself: curves acquire tangent slopes and enclosed areas — the questions only calculus can answer — handing off to Differential Calculus, with Multivariable Calculus named as the dimension-climbing sequel.
plannedLessons: The Book in One Page: the Coordinate Map
The Doorstep: Curves Acquire Slopes and Areas

books.title: Trigonometry
books.subtitle: The triangle measured, the circle’s functions — the periodic family
books.level: Class 9–12 trigonometry → the calculus doorstep
books.description: The book of the great periodic family. Angles generalized from triangles to rotation and measured in radians; the six trigonometric functions built on the unit circle with their graphs, periodicity and allied-angle machinery; the transformation formulas (compound angles, products and sums, multiple angles, conditional identities) all derived before use; general solutions of trigonometric equations with the lost-solutions discipline; the inverse functions with their principal values; the triangle fully measured — sine and cosine rules, half-angle formulas, solutions of triangles and every centre and circle; and the heights-and-distances applications. One honest note recorded: the Drive module’s logarithm chapter belongs to Advanced Algebra’s exponential book and is cross-referenced, never duplicated. Cross-references Geometry, Advanced Algebra and Coordinate Geometry; hands off to Differential Calculus.

chapters.title: Angles and Their Measures
chapters.summary: The chapter that generalizes the angle: from the acute triangle angle to rotation, measured in degrees and in radians — the arc-length definition that makes π the natural unit — with conversions, the relation between radians and real numbers, arc length and sector area. The reason radians win: the derivative formulas of calculus demand them, said now and cashed in Differential Calculus.
plannedLessons: From Triangles to Rotation: the Generalized Angle

chapters.title: Trigonometric Functions and Their Graphs
chapters.summary: The six functions built twice — first as right-triangle ratios (with the standard-angle table), then honestly as circular functions of any angle: signs by quadrant, the unit-circle definitions, periodicity read off the graph of each family, and the allied-angle machinery (n × 90° ± θ, even and odd cases). The fundamental identities (sin² + cos² = 1 and kin) proved from the circle, not memorized.
plannedLessons: Ratios of Acute Angles and the Standard Table
The Unit Circle: Functions of Any Angle
Allied Angles: the n × 90° ± θ Machine

chapters.title: The Transformation Formulas
chapters.summary: The algebra of the family: compound-angle formulas for sine and cosine derived geometrically, then tangent; the expression a cos x + b sin x as a single shifted wave; product-to-sum and sum-to-product transformations; multiple and submultiple angles; the typical-angle value techniques; sums of sines/cosines in arithmetic progression; conditional identities; and range-hunting by trigonometric substitution — the JEE heartland, all derived before use.
plannedLessons: Compound Angles: the Sum and Difference Formulas
a cos x + b sin x: the Shifted Wave

chapters.title: Trigonometric Equations
chapters.summary: Solving in a family that repeats: the general solutions of sin x = sin α, cos x = cos α, tan x = tan α; squared-function equations; the a cos x + b sin x = c type with its existence condition; equations solved by exploiting maxima and minima; graphical solutions; and trigonometric inequalities — the module’s full arc, with the lost-solutions discipline (squaring and dividing hazards) taught explicitly.
plannedLessons: Squared and Mixed Forms, and the Existence Condition

chapters.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
chapters.summary: Advanced Algebra’s inverse-machine theory cashed on the periodic family: why no trig function is invertible as-is, the principal-value restrictions, the graphs of all six inverses, the f(f⁻¹(x)) and f⁻¹(f(x)) principal-value discipline, relations among the inverses (negatives, reciprocals, complementary angles), sums and differences expressed as a single inverse, multiple angles, and substitution techniques — the NCERT class 12 arc at JEE depth. The principal values of sec⁻¹(sec x), cosec⁻¹(cosec x) and cot⁻¹(cot x) — the classic exam discipline the module’s chapter drills — named explicitly.
plannedLessons: Why the inverses need principal values
The Principal-Value Discipline: f⁻¹(f(x)) and f(f⁻¹(x))
Sums, Differences and Multiple Angles as One Inverse

chapters.title: Properties of Triangles
chapters.summary: The triangle fully measured: the sine rule with its radius-of-circumcircle form, Napier’s formula and the m–n theorem, the cosine and projection rules, half-angle formulas, the area in its many forms, the complete solution-of-triangles census (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, the ambiguous SSA, AAA), and the triangle’s centres and circles — circumcircle, incircle, excentral, orthocentre and centroid, pedal and orthic triangles — the classic Loney heartland, every formula derived. The centres named with their radii — the circumcentre with the circumcircle’s R, the incentre with the incircle’s r, the exradii of the excircles — and the centroid with its medians, the medians’ 2:1 division priced exactly.
plannedLessons: The Sine Rule and Its Consequences
Half-Angle Formulas and the Area of a Triangle
Solutions of Triangles: the Six Cases
Centres and Circles of a Triangle
The Orthocentre, Centroid and the Pedal Triangle
The Excircles: Excentres, Exradii and Their Distances

chapters.title: Heights and Distances
chapters.summary: The classic application: angles of elevation and depression, towers and objects, two-observation stations, the ambiguous cases, and the craft problems aptitude exams love. Kept honestly with the note that the current JEE Main list no longer names heights and distances — the chapter stands on its fundamentals value and its aptitude-exam reach (Khattar QA ch. 36 owns the speed-work side). Loney’s dip of the horizon — the radius-and-height model that ties small angles to the sphere you stand on — banked as the classic closing application.
plannedLessons: Elevation, Depression and the Right Setup
Two Stations and the Ambiguous Cases
Ratios of Small Angles and the Dip of the Horizon

chapters.title: The Synthesis and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The closing synthesis: competition trigonometry at speed (identity cascades, inverse-value equations, the maxima/minima of trigonometric expressions, triangle problems with the centres), the book in one page (the formula map from radians to solutions of triangles), and the doorstep itself: the periodic family is calculus’s next customer — sin x’s slope puzzle named as the question Differential Calculus answers first.
plannedLessons: The Book in One Page: the Formula Map
The Doorstep: the Periodic Family Meets the Slope

books.title: Differential Calculus
books.subtitle: How the output changes — the first calculus course
books.level: Class 11–12 differential calculus → the analysis doorstep

The whole ladder in one view: the twenty-six earlier books’ doorstep chains drawn as a single map from counting to the Lebesgue theory. The research standard of proof: the proof genres compared, the paper’s anatomy, proof critique practised on classic subtle errors. Problem-solving at the frontier: the olympiad arsenal at speed, the Putnam-style cross-boundary problems, and how a question becomes a theorem. The unifying lenses — structure, symmetry, mapping — with category theory described accurately and never mystified. The great open problems presented as doors with their verified status (Riemann, P versus NP, Navier–Stokes, Goldbach, twin primes, Collatz). And the reading-writing-entering craft for research mathematics, closing with the other disciplines’ mathematical needs mapped back to the shelf. Cross-references every book on the shelf; hands off to the graduate frontier.

chapters.title: The Ladder in One View
chapters.summary: The whole mathematics shelf as one climb: counting and place value (Foundation Mathematics) through the number systems (ANS), the algebra arc (Elementary and Advanced), geometry’s proof discipline and the analytic lines (Coordinate Geometry, Trigonometry), the calculus sequence (Differential, Integral, Multivariable, Differential Equations), the structural books (Linear and Abstract Algebra, Discrete Mathematics, Number Theory, Set Theory, Logic, Combinatorics), the probabilistic pair (Probability, Statistics), and the depth rungs (Real and Complex Analysis, Topology, Numerical Analysis, Methods, Operations Research) — each book’s doorstep-to-doorstep chain drawn as the single map it became.
plannedLessons: The Doorstep Chain, Traced End to End

chapters.title: The Standard of Proof at Research Level
chapters.summary: The craft’s highest register: the proof genres across the shelf compared (the Euclidean two-column, the ε-δ template, the diagram-chase, the counting argument, the structural proof), the writing discipline of papers (theorem–proof–remark anatomy, the hypothesis’s honest load), proof critique PRACTISED (classic subtle errors analyzed — induction’s off-by-one, the divergent-series trap, the overlooked boundary case), and the referee’s eye as the final standard.

chapters.title: Problem-Solving at the Frontier
chapters.summary: The six levels’ capstone: the olympiad craft’s full arsenal (the invariants, extremal principle, clever bijections, the generating-function reflex — Combinatorics’ engines at competition speed), the Putnam-style integration (problems that cross book boundaries — algebra wearing analysis’s coat, geometry speaking number theory), Polya’s heuristics at the frontier, and the research problem’s anatomy (how a question becomes a conjecture becomes a theorem).
plannedLessons: Polya’s Method: Understand, Plan, Execute, Look Back
How a Question Becomes a Theorem

chapters.title: Structure, Symmetry, Mapping
chapters.summary: The unifying lenses named honestly: structure (the algebraic census — group, ring, field, vector space, topological space — as ONE idea: axioms priced on examples), symmetry (the group action reading — Geometry’s figures, the polynomial’s Galois group, physics’s conservation laws named ahead), and mapping (the structure-preserving function as mathematics’s true verb), closing with category theory described accurately — objects and morphisms, the functor’s career — as the mathematician’s second-order language, its power and its limits both stated.
plannedLessons: Structure: the Axioms as One Idea

chapters.title: The Great Open Problems
chapters.summary: The doors presented with verified status: the Riemann hypothesis (unproven — the zeta function’s zeros and the primes’ music, Complex Analysis’s doorstep cashed), P versus NP (unsolved — the counting and computation books’ shared question), Navier–Stokes (open — the equation the Methods book solves in special cases), Goldbach and the twin primes (unproven, with Zhang’s 2013 bounded-gaps breakthrough and the Maynard–Tao refinements noted accurately), Collatz (unproven), and the honest lesson: the shelf’s reader now stands where the map ends and the territory begins.

chapters.title: Reading and Writing Research Mathematics
chapters.summary: The literature’s craft: how a paper is actually read (the three-pass protocol — abstract–structure–details), the literature’s anatomy (journals, the arXiv named honestly, monographs, the survey as the newcomer’s friend), mathematical writing’s standards (LaTeX named as the medium, the notation’s discipline), and the collaboration-and-seminar culture described for the entering student — with the shelf’s books mapped to the standard first graduate texts they lead into.
plannedLessons: Typesetting Mathematics: TeX and the Written Look

chapters.title: The Doorstep Beyond
chapters.summary: The final chapter of the mathematics shelf: the graduate landscape’s honest map (pure — analysis, algebra, geometry/topology, logic; applied — numerics, OR, probability/statistics; the interdisciplinary bridges), the other ten disciplines’ mathematical needs mapped to the shelf’s books (physics’s Methods, computer science’s Discrete Mathematics and Logic, economics’s Optimization — the cross-shelf handoffs made explicit), and the closing page — the reader who started at counting now owns the language; what remains is to speak something new in it.

books.title: Quantitative Aptitude
books.subtitle: The competitive-exam arithmetic family — models at speed
books.level: Aptitude arithmetic — the exam family from school maths to the world’s competitive tests
books.description: The book of the commercial-aptitude family: the model arithmetic the world’s competitive exams actually test. Percentage as the working scale; profit and loss with marked price, successive, true and banker’s discounts; simple and compound interest as the two growth models, depreciation, stocks, shares and debentures; partnership, problems on ages, alligation and mixtures; time and work with pipes and cisterns as rate problems; time, speed and distance with trains, boats and streams and races; weighted averages and the number-series craft; the mensuration census at exam speed (cross-referenced — Geometry owns the derivations, Statistics owns data interpretation); and data sufficiency as a decision discipline cross-referencing Mathematical Logic. Foundation Mathematics and the theory shelf own the concepts; this book owns their exam-craft register, the Khattar census’s missing home. Cross-references the whole shelf; hands off to every book it borrows from.

chapters.title: The Aptitude Landscape
chapters.summary: The census chapter: what the world’s aptitude exams actually test — one arithmetic family examined at speed under time pressure — and the craft that speed demands. Simplification with BODMAS/brackets discipline, approximation and estimation before any computation, digit sense (last-digit and digit-sum checks), and the honest place of shortcut methods: each shortcut derived once from the underlying algebra so the reader knows when it holds and when it betrays. Foundation Mathematics owns the operations as concepts; this chapter owns their exam-speed craft.
plannedLessons: The World’s Aptitude Exams: One Arithmetic Family
Simplification and the Order of Operations Craft

chapters.title: Percentage, Profit and Loss, and Discount
chapters.summary: The merchant family built on the percentage scale: cost, marked and selling price; profit and loss as fractions of the cost; successive transactions and the dishonest-dealer problems (false weights and scales); marked price with single and successive discounts; true discount versus banker’s discount on bills of exchange — the classic pair exam books carry. Percentage as a concept belongs to Foundation Mathematics; here it is the working scale of the entire commercial family.
plannedLessons: Price, Consumption, Population and the Inverse Percentage Family
Profit and Loss: Cost, Marked and Selling Price
Dishonest Dealers: False Weights and Scales

chapters.title: Interest and the Money Family
chapters.summary: Money growing in time: simple interest as linear (proportional) growth, compound interest as geometric growth — the two models derived and contrasted, the n-fold and fraction-of-year cases, the difference between them priced exactly; depreciation as decay at compound rates; effective and nominal rates; and the exam classics of stocks, shares and debentures — face value, market value, dividend, brokerage and yield — the vocabulary every banking and recruitment exam assumes — with annuities priced as the interest family’s steady payout member.
plannedLessons: Stocks, Shares, Debentures, Annuities and Dividends

chapters.title: Ratio, Partnership, Ages and Mixtures
chapters.summary: The proportion family in its commercial dress: ratio and proportion revisited at exam speed (Foundation Mathematics owns the concept); partnership — capital invested for different times, the proceeds split in the ratio of capital-months, sleeping and working partners with salaries; problems on ages as linear equations in time with the invariants (birth-year constants) that make them solvable; and alligation — the cross-diagram for mixtures, replacement problems and the weighted-average bridge, derived once so the cross is never magic.
plannedLessons: Ratio and Proportion at Exam Speed
Problems on Ages: Linear Equations in Time

chapters.title: Time and Work
chapters.summary: Work as a rate: the one-day unit (if A finishes in a days, each day buys 1/a of the work), combined rates added exactly as Differential Equations will formalize for flows; efficiency — the faster worker does more per day, the exchange between men and days; pipes and cisterns with filling and draining pipes (negative rates) and the emptying time; work and wages split by work done. Every problem reducible to: rate sums to one job — the chapter teaches the reduction, not the memorized cases.
plannedLessons: Work Rates and the One-Day Unit
Pipes and Cisterns: Fill and Drain
Efficiency, Men and Days, Work and Wages

chapters.title: Time, Speed and Distance
chapters.summary: The travel family: the d = st triangle and its proportionality (same distance — time inversely proportional to speed); average speed as the harmonic mean — derived, so the 2xy/(x+y) trap is understood; relative speed for approaching and receding bodies; trains crossing poles, platforms and each other (the length matters — the honest unit of distance is train-plus-obstacle); boats and streams with upstream and downstream effective speeds; races and games of skill — head starts, dead heats, linear and circular tracks, and the geometry of meeting again on a track (cross-referencing Coordinate Geometry and the circle).
plannedLessons: Speed, Distance and Time: the Proportion Triangle

chapters.title: Averages and Series at Exam Speed
chapters.summary: Two craft families on banked ground: weighted averages — the alligation bridge from chapter 4 now used in reverse, averages of combined groups, inclusion and exclusion changing an average (the sum-conservation discipline); and the number-series puzzles of aptitude papers — arithmetic and geometric patterns (Advanced Algebra owns the theory), differences and second differences, mixed and twin series, odd-one-out — solved as pattern-hunting with the derivations, not guesswork. Averages as a statistical concept belong to Statistics; this is the exam-craft register.
plannedLessons: Odd Ones Out and Twin Series

chapters.title: Clocks and Calendars
chapters.summary: The two time machines of aptitude arithmetic. The clock face as a rate problem: the minute hand gains 5.5° per minute over the hour hand — every angle, overlap, coincidence and opposite case priced from that one rate; the faulty clock (fast, slow, right twice a day) and the clocks-set-at-different-hours craft. Calendar arithmetic: the odd-day method (365 = 52 weeks + 1 odd day; the leap year adds one more), the day-of-the-week machine, the century-year rule (400 vs 100), and the date-comparison craft — leap years counted honestly between any two dates. Khattar’s dedicated chapter, every shortcut derived from the rate arithmetic beneath it.
plannedLessons: The Clock Face: Angles, Overlaps and Faulty Clocks
Calendar Arithmetic: Odd Days and Leap Years

chapters.title: Mensuration at Exam Speed
chapters.summary: The formula census at exam speed: perimeter and area of the standard plane figures (triangle in its forms, quadrilaterals, circle, sector and segment — cross-referencing Geometry chapter 8, which owns Heron and the derivations); volume and surface area of the standard solids — cube, cuboid, cylinder, cone, sphere and hemisphere (Geometry chapter 9 owns the derivations); combined solids (cone on cylinder, hemisphere on cone) and inscribed/circumscribed figures; cutting and reshaping problems where volume is conserved. The theory is cross-referenced, never re-derived here — this chapter owns the speed census.
plannedLessons: Perimeter and Area: the Exam Census
Volume and Surface Area: the Standard Solids

chapters.title: Data Sufficiency: the Decision Craft
chapters.summary: The decision format itself: a question and two statements, each labelled sufficient-or-not — the craft of never solving what you need only to DECIDE about. The statement-question contract (what is actually asked, exactly what would count as an answer), the two-statement discipline (each alone, then together — the three-verdict table), the trap census (the statement that is sufficient but not obviously so; the pair insufficient together; the value-versus-yes/no question). Sufficiency is truth-condition reasoning — cross-referencing Mathematical Logic — and the honest exam note: the format lives in MAT/NMAT-style papers and in the GMAT’s Data Insights section after the Focus edition moved it out of plain quant.

chapters.title: Modern Maths at Aptitude Speed
chapters.summary: The CAT/SSC ‘modern maths’ block as its own exam-speed layer, cross-referencing the shelf’s full treatments: set-theory word models and the two- and three-set Venn counting craft every aptitude paper leans on (the theory lives in Set Theory); functions, logarithms and inequalities at solving speed (Advanced Algebra’s chapters own the depth); permutations, combinations and probability compressed into the exam’s sixty-second patterns (Advanced Algebra’s counting chapter and Probability Theory own the proofs); and heights and distances at the right-triangle gallop (Trigonometry’s chapter owns the full discipline). Aggarwal’s and Arun Sharma’s unit censuses are the source of the block’s existence; no duplication — the shelf books are cited at every turn.
plannedLessons: Set Theory and Venn Diagrams: the Counting Craft
Functions, Logarithms and Inequalities at Exam Speed
Permutations and Combinations at Exam Speed
Heights and Distances at Exam Speed

chapters.title: The Synthesis and the Doorstep
chapters.summary: The closing synthesis: the craft map — which model answers which question (percentage or ratio? simple or compound? rate-addition or relative speed?) and the recognition drills that move it from conscious to automatic; the book in one page (the model table from simplification to data sufficiency); and the doorstep: aptitude arithmetic is the applied face of the whole mathematics shelf — the models are linear and geometric growth (Algebra and Advanced Algebra), rates (Differential Equations), means (Statistics), and the reader who wants the depth already owns the doors to every one of them.
plannedLessons: The Craft Map: Which Model When
The Book in One Page: the Model Table
The Doorstep: Aptitude Meets the Full Shelf
